title: Perpetual check: the draw you can force
outcomes: Finds the check that starts a perpetual when the side to move is behind
Plays the checking line until the position repeats
Counts the king's flight squares and checks that the queen cannot be captured
Does not take a perpetual when a better move exists

steps.text: A **perpetual check** is a series of checks that the king cannot escape, so the same position keeps returning. When a position occurs three times, a player can claim a draw (see *L-FND-SPECIAL-1*). When you are worse, a perpetual can save half a point. It works only if the king has nowhere to hide, so **test the king's squares** before you rely on it.

steps.caption: White to move. Black is ahead (a queen and three pawns against a queen), so White looks for checks.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn with check. The king has only one legal move.
Forced: g8 and g7 are covered by the queen.
Check again. The king has one square again.
Forced. The queen can go back to f7.
The position after the first check is back, for the second time. A third time allows a draw claim.

claims.statement: Qxf7+ is the engine's first choice.
The engine rates the position as equal (depth 16).
After Qxf7+ the king on h7 has exactly one legal move.
No black piece attacks the queen on f7.
After Qxf7+ Kh8 Qf8+ the king on h8 again has exactly one legal move (h7).
After five moves the queen is on f7 again.
And the black king is on h7 again.

steps.text:
Three tests before you rely on a perpetual.
**Where can the king go?** Count its flight squares after each check.
**Can the checker be captured, or the check blocked?**
**Is the draw really your best result?** If another move wins, or the perpetual is not there, a draw may be a mistake. *Rule of thumb:* take the perpetual only when the alternatives are worse.
